title: A Humble King Confronts the Temple
overview: Jesus enters Jerusalem to cheering crowds, disrupts the business in the temple, and is challenged by the city's religious leaders about who gave him the right to act.

parts.label: Arriving on a borrowed colt (vv. 1-11)
parts.note: Riding a young donkey recalled an old promise of a humble king coming to Jerusalem (Zechariah 9:9), and spreading cloaks and branches was how people welcomed royalty. 'Hosanna' was a Hebrew cry meaning 'save us' that had become a shout of praise, and the crowd's words come from Psalm 118, sung by pilgrims at the festivals.

parts.label: A fig tree with only leaves (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Mark wraps this story around the temple scene, and most scholars read it as an acted-out warning, since the prophets used a fruitless fig tree as a picture of God finding no fruit among his people (Jeremiah 8:13). Mark's own remark that it was not fig season suggests the point is symbolic, though readers have long found the episode puzzling.

parts.label: Overturning tables in the temple (vv. 15-19)
parts.note: The temple's outer court, where non-Jews were allowed to pray, held a market selling animals for sacrifice and money changers swapping coins for the special temple currency. Quoting the prophets, Jesus says God's house was meant for prayer by all nations but had become a 'den of robbers', a hideout where wrongdoers feel safe, and the leaders begin plotting his death.

parts.label: Faith and forgiveness (vv. 20-25)
parts.note: When the withered tree is noticed, Jesus turns it into teaching about bold trust in God, and some scholars think 'this mountain' hints at the temple hill while others see a common picture of the impossible. He ties prayer to forgiving others; a verse 26 repeating this point is missing from the earliest manuscripts, so many Bibles leave it out.

parts.label: Who gave you this right? (vv. 27-33)
parts.note: The temple leaders demand to know who authorized his actions, and Jesus answers with a question about John the Baptist, the popular prophet who had pointed people toward Jesus. If they say John was sent by God, they must explain why they ignored him, and if they deny it, the crowd will turn on them, so they claim not to know and Jesus declines to answer too.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jesus' actions in the temple were mainly a call to reform and purify worship there, or a symbolic announcement that the temple system itself was coming to an end.
think: When something looks impressive from a distance but turns out empty up close, what helps you tell the difference, whether in an institution or in yourself?
